title: Hello, Blob!
tagline: Run your first program and put something alive on the screen.
builtOn: Nothing. This is where we start.
goals: Open Processing and run a sketch
Explain that `setup()` runs **once** and `draw()` runs **over and over**
Create a `Blob` from the SpriteGame library and put it on screen
Use RGB numbers to pick any color you want

vocab.def: the function Processing runs one time, right when your sketch starts
the function Processing runs over and over, about 60 times every second
a thing in your program that has its own information and knows how to do things
something an object knows how to do. You call it with a dot: `myBlob.drawSprite()`
the three numbers (Red, Green, Blue) that describe any color. Each one goes from 0 to 255

warmup: Have you ever seen code before? What do you think it looks like? There is no wrong answer here.

p: Every Processing sketch is built out of two functions, and you will use them in every single lesson from here on.
`setup()` is like setting up an art table. It happens **once**, before anything else. You put out your paper and your paints, and then you are done setting up.
`draw()` is like drawing one page of a flipbook. Processing runs it again, and again, and again — roughly **60 times a second**. Flip those pages fast enough and it looks like motion.
bullets: Something that happens one time? It goes in `setup()`.
Something that has to keep happening? It goes in `draw()`.

p: A `Blob` is an object — a thing that lives in your program. To make one you fill in five pieces of information:

code.label: Reading the Blob line

bullets: `x` and `y` are where the **center** of the blob sits. `(0, 0)` is the top-left corner of the window.
The **radius** is half the blob's width. A radius of 40 makes a circle 80 pixels across.
`this` means "this sketch." Copy it exactly and never change it.

p: `color(255, 80, 80)` means: a lot of red, a little green, a little blue. That comes out as a warm pink-red.
Each number goes from **0** (none of that color) to **255** (as much as possible). `color(0, 0, 0)` is black. `color(255, 255, 255)` is white.
You do not have to guess. Open **Tools → Color Selector**, click around until you find a color you like, and read the R, G, and B numbers right off the panel.
`background(255)` paints the whole window white. It is inside `draw()` because it has to happen on **every single frame** — it wipes the previous picture away so the next one starts clean.
Try taking it out later and see what happens. It is a good surprise.

steps: Open Processing. You get an empty window with a big text area, a **▶ Run** button, and a **■ Stop** button.
Save the sketch first: **File → Save As**, and name it `HelloBlob`.
Type or paste in the starter code below. Getting it exactly right matters — one missing semicolon and it will not run.
Press **▶ Run**. A window should open with a red circle in the middle. Press **■ Stop** to close it.
Change the radius from `40` to `80` and run again. Then try `15`. Watch what changes.
Open **Tools → Color Selector**. Pick a color you like and read its R, G, and B numbers. Put those three numbers into `color( , , )` and run.
Move your blob: change the `400` and the `300` to put it somewhere else in the window.
Change `background(255)` to `background(0)` and run. What happened, and why?

code.label: Main sketch tab

makeItYours: Change your blob's color using **Tools → Color Selector**. Pick one you actually like.
Change its size. Try a radius of `20`, then `80`. Which one feels right?
Move it somewhere else on the screen — a corner, the top, off to one side.
Change the background color to something other than white.
Add a **second blob** with its own color and its own spot. You will need a second variable, a second `new Blob(...)` in `setup()`, and a second `drawSprite()` in `draw()`.
challenge: Arrange four or five blobs into a small scene — a face, a snowman, a planet with moons, whatever you see in them.
flintHint: Good things to ask: "my sketch will not run and it says cannot find class Blob", "how do I pick a color?", or "what is the difference between setup and draw?" Tell it you are on Lesson 1.
wrapup: What are the two magic functions, and when does each one run?
assignmentTask: Get the Lesson 1 sketch running, then change your blob so it is unmistakably yours.
assignmentDo: Run the starter sketch and get a Blob on screen.
Change **at least one thing on purpose** — color, size, position, or background.
Be ready to say **why** you chose it. "Because I like green" is a perfectly good reason. "I clicked randomly" is not.
submit: A screenshot of your sketch running.
Your answer to **Show your thinking** below (type it in the comment box).
checklist: Run a sketch with **▶** and stop it with **■**.
Point to my Blob on the screen.
Say which code runs **once** (`setup`) and which runs **over and over** (`draw`).
Change something about my blob on purpose, so it feels like **mine**.
standard: Create and display a `Blob`, using `setup()`/`draw()` and RGB color.

stages.name: Getting Started
stages.text: My sketch is not running yet, or no blob appears. **Next step:** check the very first line. A missing `import coxprogramming.processing.sprites.*;` is the number one reason a sketch will not run. Fix it and run again.

stages.name: Got It Working
stages.text: My sketch runs and a Blob appears on screen.

stages.name: Made It Mine
stages.text: …and I deliberately changed at least one thing — color, size, position, or background — and I can say **why** I chose it.

stages.name: Went Beyond
stages.text: …and I added a second blob with its own color and place, or arranged several blobs into a small scene of my own.

thinking: In one or two sentences: what did you change, and what is one thing you would try with more time?

p: Project the IDE. Point at the Run and Stop buttons, the text area, and the tab bar (they will need the tab bar in Lesson 2).

di.h: setup vs draw — use the metaphor
p: `setup()` = setting up the art table once. `draw()` = drawing a new page of a flipbook every fraction of a second.
Establish this now and reinforce it in every single lesson. Students should eventually predict without thinking: one-time things in `setup()`, repeating things in `draw()`.
"This tells Processing we want to use the library's tools." That is the whole explanation. Do not go further.

di.h: Walk the Blob constructor parameter by parameter
bullets: `this` means "this sketch." Tell them to copy it exactly and never change it.
`x` and `y` place the **center** of the blob.
`radius` is how big — half the width.
`color()` takes three numbers: how much red, green, and blue.

di.h: Color and RGB — do not skip this
p: Spend real time here. Open **Tools → Color Selector** on the projector, pick a color, and show students where to read the R, G, and B values off the panel.

Most of the personalization in this lesson (and the enthusiasm for it) comes from students discovering they can have *any* color. Make sure every student knows the Color Selector exists before they start working.
Change `background(255)` to `background(0)` live. White vs. black. Then, if you want a good moment, comment `background()` out entirely and add a moving blob later in Lesson 3 to show the smear.

guided: Everyone opens Processing and saves a new sketch as `HelloBlob` **before** typing anything. Saving first avoids the "where did my file go" problem later.
Type the starter code together on the projector, line by line. Typing beats pasting here — they need to feel the syntax once.
Everyone runs it. Circulate. The two failures you will see are a missing import line and a missing semicolon.
Together: change the radius to `80`, run, change to `15`, run. Name what changed.
Open the Color Selector as a class. Each student picks a color and puts their own RGB numbers in.
Release them to move the blob, change the background, and try a second blob.
pitfalls: **Missing import line.** By far the most common. The sketch will not compile and the error message does not point at the missing import.
Changing `this` to something else. Tell them up front it is off limits.
Putting `myBlob = new Blob(...)` inside `draw()` — it technically runs, but it rebuilds the object 60 times a second. Worth catching now.
Forgetting the semicolon at the end of a line.
Expecting `color(255, 80, 80)` to be quoted like text. It is three numbers, no quotes.
teacher.wrapupAnswer: `setup()` runs once at the start; `draw()` runs over and over, about 60 times a second. Students should be able to say this without prompting by the end of the period.
notes: The no-velocity constructor `Blob(this, x, y, radius, color)` is used deliberately. Velocity is Lesson 3.
Students **will** ask "how do I make it move?" That is exactly the reaction you want. Tell them that is next time.
If a student finishes very early, push them toward a scene made of several blobs rather than more fiddling with one.
Do not explain what an object *is* in any depth. They made one and it showed up. That is enough for today.
